title: How Sanjeev Kapoor's Parents Shaped India's Most Famous Chef
excerpt: From an Ambala boy who didn't know what a chef was to a Padma Shri-winning culinary icon — Kapoor credits his parents' unconventional support and values for his extraordinary journey.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Sanjeev Kapoor's parents supported his unconventional career choice in hotel management during the 1980s.
  • His father's job exposed Kapoor to diverse cuisines, shaping his culinary journey.
  • Kapoor's mother emphasized simple, seasonal vegetarian cooking, influencing his restaurant and cookbook philosophy.
  • Now a father, Kapoor encourages parents to trust and learn from their children.

  • Sanjeev Kapoor's parents backed his unconventional choice of hotel management in the 1980s, when medicine and engineering were the only socially accepted careers in India.
  • His father's transferable State Bank of India job exposed the family to diverse regional cuisines and cultures across cities like Delhi, Meerut, and Saharanpur — a formative influence on Kapoor's palate.
  • Kapoor's mother instilled a love for simple, seasonal vegetarian cooking that continues to anchor his culinary philosophy across 59 restaurants and 150-plus cookbooks.
  • Now a father of two, Kapoor applies the same parenting approach — telling parents to "believe in your children and learn from them."

When Sanjeev Kapoor filled out an extra hotel management admission form that his friend Jasmit Singh handed him in the early 1980s, he had no idea what a chef even did. "Nobody from my family had ever been to restaurants," he has said. "I didn't even know what the word chef meant or how it was pronounced."

Three decades later, Kapoor is India's most recognized culinary name — the host of Khana Khazana, Asia's longest-running cookery show that aired for 18 years across 120 countries, the owner of 59 restaurants, the author of more than 150 cookbooks, and a Padma Shri recipient. But behind this sprawling empire lies a quieter story: two middle-class parents in Ambala, Haryana, who gave their son the freedom to chart his own path.

A Childhood of Transfers and Open Minds

Born on April 10, 1964, in Ambala, Kapoor grew up in a household defined by his father's career at the State Bank of India. The job brought regular transfers — Delhi, Meerut, Saharanpur, back to Delhi — and with each move came exposure to new cities, schools, and crucially, new food cultures.

Kapoor attended St. Thomas School in Meerut, St. Mary's Academy in Saharanpur, and a government school in Delhi's Rajouri Garden from ninth grade onward. The constant relocation could have been unsettling, but Kapoor has described it as liberating.

"My parents inculcated in us all the important values — honesty, hard work, humility, being respectful to others. They did not preach all this to us. We learned by watching what they practiced."

— Sanjeev Kapoor, in an interview with ParentCircle

His father was "always keen on learning new things," according to Kapoor — a trait the son clearly inherited. His mother cooked simple vegetarian meals with seasonal produce and a deft hand with spices. "She knows what to use and how much to put in what, and her dish always turns out right, every time," Kapoor told Culinate. That emphasis on fresh ingredients and unfussy technique would later become a hallmark of his own cooking style.

When the 'Accidental Chef' Chose His Path

In 1980s India, career options for middle-class families rarely extended beyond medicine and engineering. Kapoor scored 80 percent in his exams — more than enough for either track — and even secured admission to the School of Planning and Architecture. But conventional paths bored him. He was the student who chose Sanskrit as his third language "because no one else did," according to The Better India.

Then came the hotel management form. It was a whim, not a calling. But Kapoor's parents responded with a clarity that still resonates.

"Don't worry about what anyone else says. If you are sure, then do what you want to do."

— Sanjeev Kapoor's parents, as recalled by the chef

"My parents knew that if I set my eyes on something, I would get the best results, so they trusted me," Kapoor has said. "Wanting to do something different was my predictable behaviour, so there was no resistance." Friends, neighbours, and extended family pushed back. His parents did not.

From Pusa Institute to Centaur Hotel

Kapoor enrolled at the Pusa Institute of Hotel Management in Delhi and graduated in 1984. He joined the India Tourism Development Corporation (ITDC) as a management trainee, rising to executive chef during a posting in Varanasi within two years. He moved to ITDC's Hotel Samrat in Delhi, then to Mumbai's Centaur Hotel group for five years.

While his peers preferred front-desk work, Kapoor chose the kitchen. By 27, he was the executive chef of Centaur Hotel in Mumbai — the youngest in the chain's history. "Head chef was the highest benchmark," he told The Better India. "I was shocked because I had peaked so early, but I never ran out of options to explore."

A Legacy of Learning
›Parents encouraged Kapoor's unique career path.
›Father's job fostered exposure to diverse food cultures.
›Mother's cooking philosophy focused on simplicity and seasonality.
›Kapoor promotes learning from children in parenting.

He pursued a Master's in Marketing Management at NMIMS Mumbai. Then television came calling. Khana Khazana, originally named Shriman Bawarchi and planned with a rotating cast of chefs, was reshaped around Kapoor after audiences responded to his screen presence in the first episode. Director Hansal Mehta and his production team changed the format, and the show ran from 1993 to 2012.

A Diaspora Kitchen Icon

For Indians who grew up abroad in the 1990s and 2000s, Kapoor was the bridge to home cooking. Khana Khazana aired across 120 countries. Kapoor's website carried over 10,000 recipes. Families from Colorado to Kuala Lumpur watched him simplify elaborate hotel dishes into home-kitchen-friendly versions.

"Wives, and even husbands, have written to me saying I have saved their marriage," Kapoor told The Better India. "I remember meeting a lady at the Colorado airport who couldn't stop thanking me for helping her settle in the family with ease after marriage."

Today, his brand extends to restaurant chains including The Yellow Chilli — with outlets in Dubai, Kuwait, and across North America — the FoodFood channel, a Singapore Airlines culinary panel seat, and a range of cookware products. In a candid 2025 conversation with journalist Vir Sanghvi, Kapoor revealed he had initially rejected MasterChef India and demanded to be paid more than Bollywood star Akshay Kumar before eventually joining the franchise.

Paying It Forward

Kapoor's parents taught by example, and he has tried to do the same. His older daughter Rachita studied law and now works in his business. Younger daughter Kriti, who studied mathematics and statistics, is a national-level sprinter. His wife Alyona Kapoor co-runs Turmeric Vision Pvt. Ltd., the company behind his brand.

Kapoor's Social Impact
›Supports Forum for Autism for over 15 years.
›Distributed 25,000 meals daily during COVID-19.
›Employs persons with autism in his companies.
›Serves as UN Ambassador for Clean Cookstoves Campaign.

He has also channeled his parents' sense of service into social work — supporting Forum for Autism for over 15 years, employing persons with autism in his companies, and serving as the United Nations' Indian Ambassador for its Clean Cookstoves Campaign. During the COVID-19 pandemic, he partnered with Akshaya Patra Foundation and IHCL to distribute over 25,000 meals daily to hospital staff across 36 hospitals in 15 cities.

"Learn from your children," Kapoor has said. "Believe in them and learn from them. They know much more than what we do." It sounds a lot like what his own parents once did for him.
